Standard negative binomial models for recurrent hospitalizations use total follow-up (or observation) time as an offset, which implicitly assumes that stopping follow-up due to death is non-informative with respect to the event process. When mortality risk differs by arm (as is typical in HF trials), this assumption is violated — patients who die stop accumulating both events and exposure time, which can differentially bias the estimated rate ratio (often favoring the arm with higher mortality, since dead patients can no longer contribute additional hospitalizations).

It estimates a ratio of rate functions (equivalent to ratio of mean cumulative functions under proportional rates), treating death as independent censoring of the counting process. As with the negative binomial approach, if death is differential between arms and related to the hospitalization risk, this creates the same bias/interpretability issue — LWYY does not explicitly model the terminal event.

By giving death top priority in the hierarchy, the terminal event is explicitly incorporated into the endpoint by design, rather than being treated as a nuisance censoring mechanism.
